slides.title: What Is a Rigid Body?
slides.text:
What Is a Rigid Body?

• A rigid body is an idealized solid object where the distance
  between any two points remains constant regardless of external
   forces.
•  In robotics: robot links (arms, legs, joints) are modeled as rigid
   bodies connected at joints.
•  Degrees of Freedom (3D)
   – 3 Translational-x, y, z displacement
   – 3 Rotational-Roll, Pitch, Yaw





                                                                                                           4

visualInspection.notes: Rigid-body idealization preserves distance between any two material points despite external forces; robot links connected at joints; unconstrained spatial body has three translational and three rotational DOFs. Printed 4.

slides.title: Dynamics of A Manipulator
slides.text:
Dynamics of A Manipulator

•  There are two problems related to the dynamics of a manipulator
   that we wish to solve
   – For given trajectory point Θ, ሶΘ and ሷΘ, find the required vector of joint
       torques 𝜏, Used for controlling the manipulator (Inverse dynamics)
   – Calculate how the mechanism will move under application of a set of joint
       torques i.e., given 𝜏, findΘ, ሶΘ and ሷΘ for the simulation (forward dynamics).





                                                                                                           5

visualInspection.notes: Inverse dynamics: given position/rate/acceleration find joint torque for control. Forward: given torque find motion for simulation; requires model and initial state beyond abbreviated slide wording. Dots on Θ clearly present. Printed 5.

MASS DISTRIBUTION

•  For a single DOF translatory motion, we talk about the
   mass of a rigid body.
•   In the case of rotational motion about a single axis, we
    talk about the moment of inertia.
•   In the case of rotation about an arbitrary axis, we need a
   complete way of characterizing the mass distribution of a
    rigid body.
•   Inertia tensors are defined with respect to a frame {𝐴}
   attached to rigid body as
                𝐼𝑥𝑥   −𝐼𝑥𝑦  −𝐼𝑥𝑧
     •  𝐴𝐼= −𝐼𝑥𝑦   𝐼𝑦𝑦   −𝐼𝑦𝑧
            −𝐼𝑥𝑧  −𝐼𝑦𝑧    𝐼𝑧𝑧

                                                                                                          10

visualInspection.notes: Mass for translation, scalar inertia for a single rotation axis, tensor for arbitrary axis. Tensor symmetric with negative raw products off diagonal. Body diagram labels dV and position vector from A origin. Printed 10.

slides.title: Parallel-axis Theorem
slides.text:
Parallel-axis Theorem

•  The parallel-axis theorem, is used to compute the inertia tensor under translations
   of the reference coordinate system.
•  The parallel-axis theorem relates the inertia tensor in a frame {𝐶} with origin at the
   center of mass to the inertia tensor with respect to another arbitrarily translated
   reference frame {𝐴} as,
  ➢ 𝐴𝐼𝑧𝑧= 𝐶𝐼𝑧𝑧+ 𝑚𝑥𝑐2 + 𝑦𝑐2  ,
  ➢ 𝐴𝐼𝑥𝑦= 𝐶𝐼𝑥𝑦−𝑚𝑥𝑐𝑦𝑐,
•  Where 𝑃𝑐=  𝑥𝑐, 𝑦𝑐, 𝑧𝑐𝑇locates the COM relative to {𝐴}.
•  The theorem may be stated in vector—matrix form as
  ➢ 𝐴𝐼= 𝐶𝐼+ 𝑚𝑃𝑐𝑇𝑃𝑐𝐼3 −𝑃𝑐𝑃𝑐𝑇
•  Robot links rotate about joint axes, not their own COM.
•   Parallel axis theorem is applied repeatedly to compute the
    effective inertia seen at each joint motor.

                                                                                                          17

visualInspection.notes: Parallel-axis matrix formula I_A=I_C+m[(pᵀp)I3−ppᵀ], p points A-origin to COM. Izz shift uses xc²+yc². Scalar Ixy formula uses minus, contrary to raw-positive product definition on362; it is consistent only as signed tensor-entry convention. Same orientation required. Printed 17.

slides.title: Mass Distribution in Robot Design
slides.text:
Mass Distribution in Robot Design

•   Distal Mass Reduction
   – Minimize mass far from the base. Reduces effective
        inertia at shoulder joints by r² factor. Enables smaller,
      cheaper motors.
• COM Placement
   – Strategic placement of batteries, actuators, and
      counterweights keeps system COM stable across all
       configurations.
•  Link Shape Optimization
   – Hollow tubes, I-beams, and lattice structures reduce
      mass while maintaining stiffness. AI-driven topology
       optimization automates this.


                                                                                                          21

visualInspection.notes: Distal mass and squared-distance inertia contribution; COM placement via batteries/actuators/counterweights; hollow tubes, I-beams, lattice and AI topology optimization. Across-all-configurations COM stability is an unqualified design aspiration, not guaranteed by placement alone. Printed 21.

slides.title: •  Balanced Design
slides.text:
•  Balanced Design
   – Symmetric mass distribution about rotation axes reduces products of inertia
   → simpler control equations.
•   Inertia Matching
  ― Motor inertia ≈ load inertia maximizes power transfer efficiency. AI tunes
       gear ratios to match this condition.
•  Agility vs Stability
  ― Less distal mass → faster motion. More proximal mass → better stability. AI
       learns optimal trade-off per task.





                                                                                                          22

visualInspection.notes: Balanced distribution reduces relevant products; inertia-matching motor≈load and AI gear ratios; agility versus stability mass-location tradeoff. Efficiency claim requires objective/model and reflected-inertia convention; not universally established. Printed 22.

slides.title: Some additional facts about inertia tensors
slides.text:
Some additional facts about inertia tensors

•   If two axes of the reference frame form a plane of symmetry for the
  mass distribution of the body, the products of inertia, having as an index
   the coordinate that is normal to the plane of symmetry, will be zero.
•  Moments of inertia must always be positive. Products of inertia may
   have either sign.
•  The sum of the three moments of inertia is invariant under orientation
   changes in the reference frame.
•  The eigenvalues of an inertia tensor are the principal
  moments for the body. The associated eigenvectors
   are the principal axes.
•  Practically M.I. is measured rather than calculated
   for each link by using a measuring device
    (e.g., an inertia pendulum).


                                                                                                          23

visualInspection.notes: Symmetry-plane products involving normal coordinate vanish; moments positive wording needs degenerate-distribution nonnegative qualification; products either sign; trace invariant under orientation only; eigenvalues/moments and eigenvectors/axes; inertia pendulum measurement example. Printed 23.

slides.title: URDF: Specifying Mass & Inertia for AI
slides.text:
URDF: Specifying Mass & Inertia for AI

           URDF XML                         •  Mass: Total link mass in kg
                                                            •  origin xyz: COM position
   <link name="forearm">
                                                           relative to link frame
    <inertial>                                                            •   ixx, iyy, izz: Principal
    <mass value="1.5"/>
                                         moments (kg·m²)
     <origin xyz="0 0 0.15" rpy="0 0 0"/>                                                            •   ixy, ixz, iyz:Products of
     <inertia
                                                           inertia (= 0 if symmetric)
      ixx="0.003" ixy="0" ixz="0"
      iyy="0.003" iyz="0"
      izz="0.001"/>
    </inertial>
   </link>

Best Practice: Use SolidWorks → export URDF plugin to auto-compute inertia from CAD geometry.

                                                                                                            24

visualInspection.notes: Actual XML forearm link: mass1.5; inertial origin xyz=0 0 .15,rpy=0 0 0; ixx=.003,iyy=.003,izz=.001,other entries0. Units kg and kg m² shown. Principal label valid for this diagonal example, not arbitrary entries. Symmetry statement requires appropriate axes. CAD/SolidWorks export suggestion at bottom. Printed 24.

sourceIssues.finding: Forward dynamics is abbreviated to torque-to-motion without explicitly listing model and initial state.
sourceIssues.handling: Questions make the omitted model/state assumptions explicit; no uniqueness from torque alone is asserted.

sourceIssues.finding: The slide presents positive definiteness and hard-constraint encoding without delimiting degenerate mass distributions or actual implementation.
sourceIssues.handling: Questions explicitly assume a nondegenerate solid for positive definiteness; mathematical nonnegativity and implementation-dependent enforcement are separated.

sourceIssues.finding: p362 defines Ixy=∫xy dm and p361 uses −Ixy in the tensor; p368 writes Ixy,A=Ixy,C−mxc yc, which is instead the signed matrix-entry rule. p369 confirms this by inserting −mwl/4. p376 repeats both conventions together.
sourceIssues.handling: Use Pxy for raw products and I12 for signed tensor entries. Derive Pxy,A=Pxy,C+mxc yc and I12,A=I12,C−mxc yc. Preserve the slide notation conflict explicitly.

sourceIssues.finding: The hollow-cylinder row mR² omits the thin-wall assumption; the plate row only says axis through center, omitting normal-to-plane direction.
sourceIssues.handling: State thin shell and central normal axis explicitly. Derive the plate row from the box limit, and do not extend mR² to arbitrary wall thickness.

sourceIssues.finding: The statements about smaller motors and COM stability across all configurations are unconditional in wording.
sourceIssues.handling: Questions treat inertia reduction as a geometric consequence under stated assumptions and motor/COM benefits as design goals requiring load, motion and configuration checks.

sourceIssues.finding: Inertia matching is called a universal efficiency maximum without a drive model or reflected-load convention; proximal mass is equated with better stability without conditions.
sourceIssues.handling: Retain the matching criterion as an explicitly source-attributed heuristic. Require stated drive coordinates/objective and treat stability/agility statements as conditional design guidance.

sourceIssues.finding: Strictly positive moments exclude ideal axis/point-supported distributions; trace invariance is stated for orientation changes, not translations. Practical measurement wording is not exclusive of the following CAD computation advice.
sourceIssues.handling: Use nonnegative squared-distance derivation for degenerate cases, keep the origin fixed for orientation invariance, and distinguish measurement from calculation without treating either as forbidden.

sourceIssues.finding: The slide calls ixx,iyy,izz principal moments and says products vanish if symmetric without stating axes.
sourceIssues.handling: The shown tensor is diagonal, so its diagonal entries are principal. General tensor components need not be eigenvalues; symmetry must be relevant to the chosen origin and axes. The actual XML is preserved and parsed without repair.

supplementalImplementationReference.scope: Official ROS documentation confirms kg mass, the symmetric six-entry matrix, and the inertial-origin frame. This supports implementation convention checks, not replacement of the supplied lecture as course authority.

sourceIssues.finding: The summary labels the coincident/zero-origin-acceleration expression as generalized but omits a0 from the general p359 equation.
sourceIssues.handling: Explicit comparison questions preserve the omission. General numerical questions use p359; summary equation is restricted to a0=0.
